contentSections: Quick answer

Wind load is the pressure that moving air puts on a facade. It pushes on the windward face and pulls on the leeward face and edges, and it grows with building height and exposure. A metal facade must be designed so the panels, fixings, sub-frame and anchors carry this load into the structure safely. This is a core part of facade engineering, and it should be calculated for each project, not copied from a standard drawing.
Key takeaways

• Wind load rises with building height. Upper floors can see pressures well above ground level. • Edges and corners usually take the highest local pressures. • The sub-frame carries the load, so it is the most critical hidden part of the facade. • Tall or unusually shaped buildings may need wind tunnel testing or computational fluid dynamics. • Metal also moves with heat, so the design must handle wind and thermal movement together.
What facade engineering covers

When people search for facade engineering or cladding engineering, they usually want to know who makes sure a facade is safe, stays attached and lasts. Facade engineering covers loads, materials, fixings, movement, water management, fabrication tolerances and installation. Our overview of how metal facade engineering works walks through the whole sequence. This article goes deeper on one part: wind.
How wind acts on a facade

• Pressure on the face that meets the wind. • Suction on side faces, the back and the roof edge. • Local peaks at corners, parapets and edges, where air speeds up and swirls. • Gusts and fluctuation, which load fixings repeatedly over years.
Because panels are thin and light, suction is often the governing case. A panel must stay in place when air pulls it outward as well as when it pushes inward.
What decides the design wind load
Several inputs go into the calculation.

1. Location and basic wind speed. Indian structural practice uses the national wind load standard, IS 875 Part 3, to set wind speeds by region. 2. Building height. Higher means greater pressure. 3. Terrain and surroundings. Open ground, coast and dense city each behave differently. 4. Building shape. Corners, projections, cantilevers and openings change pressure zones. 5. Panel size and position. Large panels near corners need stronger fixing.

For tall or irregular buildings, code-based calculations may miss localised pressure zones. In those cases engineers use wind tunnel testing or computational fluid dynamics to find them. Always follow the current code and your structural consultant’s advice.
From wind pressure to fixings
Once the pressure is known, the engineer works backwards through each element.

ElementQuestion the engineer answers
PanelIs the sheet thick and stiff enough, or does it need folded edges or stiffeners?
FixingsDo the fixings hold at the worst suction, with a safety margin?
Sub-frame railsAre rail size and spacing right for the span?
Brackets and anchorsDoes the structural wall or slab take the load?
JointsDo they allow movement without opening or rattling?

For flat panels, Metaguise offers 2.0 mm, 2.5 mm and 3.0 mm solid aluminium gauges. The 3.0 mm gauge is used for high-wind-load locations and oversized formats, while 2.5 mm suits primary exterior commercial facades. Details are in our SolidPanel guide.
Wind and heat together

Metal expands and contracts with daily and seasonal temperature change. If a design locks panels rigidly, movement builds stress at fixings and shows up as noise, waves or fatigue cracks. Good designs let panels move in controlled directions while still resisting wind. On the Miraj Stadium facade in Rajasthan, edge and corner wind loads and summer heat were designed together, with joints that allow movement without buckling or noise. Read the Miraj Stadium project story.

Different conditions can also change the design on the same building. At the Nadaun indoor stadium in Himachal Pradesh, altitude-related temperature swings required substructures that absorb movement without passing stress to neighbouring bands. See the Nadaun stadium facade.
Open systems and wind

In ventilated systems with an air gap, wind pressure can also act inside the cavity and on the layers behind the cladding. This is one reason to evaluate the full system and not only the panel. Our article on ventilated metal systems explains the cavity principle.
Questions to ask your facade company about wind

• Which code and wind speed did you use for this location? • Are edges and corners designed for higher local pressure? • Who signs off the structural calculations? • Will you share a fixing and sub-frame detail before production? • Do you recommend a mock-up or a test for this building?
Common mistakes

• Using one standard fixing for the whole elevation, with no extra at corners. • Ignoring suction and checking only inward pressure. • Choosing panel thickness on looks alone. • No movement allowance, so heat and wind loads combine badly.
Frequently asked questions

1. What is wind load on a facade?

It is the pressure and suction that wind applies to the facade surface, which the panels, fixings and sub-frame must carry safely to the structure.

2. Does wind load matter for houses, or only tall buildings?

It matters for every building, but it grows with height and exposure, so taller and more open sites need closer checks.

3. Which part of a facade sees the highest wind load?

Edges, corners and parapets usually see higher local pressure than the middle of a flat wall.

4. What is facade engineering?

It is the design discipline that makes a facade safe, durable and buildable, covering loads, materials, fixings, movement, water and installation.

5. When is wind tunnel testing needed?

For tall buildings or unusual shapes where standard code calculations may miss local pressure zones, engineers may use wind tunnel testing or computational fluid dynamics.

6. Who is responsible for facade structural design?

Usually the facade company’s engineers design the facade and its fixings, and the building’s structural engineer checks the load on the structure. Agree responsibilities in writing.
